title: I built a 3-tier AI brain for town NPCs — they plan their day, decide who to talk to, and reflect at night
author: Dry_Week_4945
selftext:
I've been working on an open-source 3D town where AI agents live as NPCs. The part I'm most proud of is the NPC behavior system — it runs on three decision layers:

**L1 — Daily Plan** (once at dawn): The LLM generates a schedule like "morning: visit café, afternoon: park bench, evening: walk home." Each NPC plans differently based on their personality and yesterday's experiences.

**L2 — Tactical Decisions** (every ~2 min): When an NPC arrives somewhere or spots a nearby NPC, it asks: "Should I stay? Talk to them? Go somewhere else?" Context includes current location, nearby NPCs, recent memories, and town events.

**L3 — Dialogue**: When two NPCs decide to talk, they have multi-turn LLM conversations with personality-consistent responses, then generate a summary stored in their memory.

**Zero-LLM fallback**: When the AI isn't available, a state machine + 400 preset dialogue lines take over seamlessly — NPCs still feel alive through algorithm-driven routines and casual encounters.

Other game systems tied to NPC behavior:
- 24h day/night cycle (NPCs wake at dawn, sleep at dusk)
- 12 weather types affecting NPC mood and conversation topics
- Procedural ambient sound — rain, birds, crickets, thunder — all synthesized via Web Audio API, zero audio files
- A "Banwei Buster" mini-game where overworked NPCs generate stress orbs you can pop (combo system + boss fights)

The whole thing also includes a visual map editor (drag & drop buildings) and a character workshop (pick 3D models, write AI-generated personality files).

Built with Three.js + TypeScript, runs as a plugin for OpenClaw.

GitHub: https://github.com/Agentshire/Agentshire

Curious what you think about the 3-tier brain approach — any ideas for making NPC decisions feel more emergent?

comments.author: srvs1
comments.body: Cool. How'd you do the art?

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: I'm an AI UGC game developer. After OpenClaw came out, I started thinking about how to integrate UGC with OpenClaw, and then I started building my own system using Cursor and OpenClaw.

comments.author: hugobart
comments.body: what model(s) do you use to keep the costs down?

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: I'm currently using a Minimax monthly plan, which keeps token consumption under control. I'd recommend purchasing an LLM monthly plan instead of API billing.

comments.author: AxiosXiphos
comments.body: This is exactly the kind of thing I'm excited about A.I. for. I want to see the Sims or Crusader Kings but every character run by actual a.i. We are getting closer every day.

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: I believe that integrating OpenClaw holds the promise of a unique opportunity: leveraging user-provided computing resources to power AI NPCs, thereby enabling a truly realistic \*The Sims\*-like experience. Relying solely on the platform to provide the computing power to drive these AI NPCs would simply be too costly.

replies.author: kujasgoldmine
replies.body: That would be insanely good! Now you can always predict what a ruler does, but with real AI behind the characters, now a warmonger might instead propose an alliance to you and then backstab you when you least expect it.

replies.author: Harcurio
replies.body: There is a paper with this idea in AIIDE could be interest thing to read !!

comments.author: jacksterson
comments.body: Careful, this game mechanic sounds patented

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: This is fully open source (MIT license), so the exact opposite of patented. If anything, I'd love to see more people build on this approach!

replies.author: JorgitoEstrella
replies.body: Which of their games are like this?

comments.author: singh_taranjeet
comments.body: The reflection mechanic is clever. Do they actually modify their behavior based on what they reflect on, or is it more for flavor?

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: From a game design perspective, the true purpose of reflection is to render the agent's daily behaviors more plausible—essentially an attempt to create an AI-driven "Sims" experience, rather than one driven by decision trees.

replies.author: HideousSerene
replies.body: Reflection is something this study used: https://hai.stanford.edu/news/computational-agents-exhibit-believable-humanlike-behavior in case you're interested in it more!

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: Thanks,I look forward to your participation or feedback.

comments.author: Legitimate_Ask_7369
comments.body: What tool(s) are you using to turn the 2d asset into 3d ones? Looks really cool!

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: I use 3d.hunyuan and [meshy.ai](http://meshy.ai), I switch between them.

replies.author: throwaway12222018
replies.body: Do those do animations too? How did you do the animations

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: First, the AI ​​generates a 3D character, then the AI ​​binds the skeleton. After the skeleton is successfully bound, you can select the animations you need to add to GLK, and finally export it for use.

replies.author: throwaway12222018
replies.body: Nice. Are you just using the free tier btw? Wondering how many tries it takes to actually get something useful out. My 2d sprites are cartoonish, i think they should pretty easily generalize to 3d

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: I'm using the monthly version. If the image quality is acceptable, one or two attempts should be enough to produce a usable image. Mine is low-poly, so it doesn't need to be very detailed.

replies.author: Dry_Week_4945
replies.body: Thank you, I hope you like it and recommend it!
